properties.title: Learning Patient-Specific Disease Dynamics with Latent Flow Matching for Longitudinal Imaging Generation
properties.membership_basis: The reported implementation encodes an observed brain MRI into a latent state, advances that state with a learned velocity field over a longitudinal progression coordinate anchored to elapsed years, and decodes a future MRI. Reported results evaluate future human MRI observations.
properties.membership_boundary: Observational organ-state forecasting, not treatment-response simulation, causal identification or planning.

properties.hash_provenance: Supplied source record; not recomputed in this call.
properties.publication_statement_printed: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026
properties.bibliographic_verification_boundary: Title-page text and supplied visual-review notes support these source-reported details; no publisher or conference site was independently checked.
properties.year_reconciliation: The source record's 2025 differs from the read v4's 2026 date and conference header. The immutable legacy cell D already records 2026.

properties.design: Retrospective longitudinal human MRI generation and forecasting benchmark with method ablations and auxiliary sensitivity analyses.
properties.disease_scope: Alzheimer's disease and associated longitudinal brain imaging; Figure 3 includes CN, MCI and AD labels.

properties.name: Progression Latent Flow Matching (∆-LFM)
properties.configuration_identity: Default configuration described in arXiv v4; checkpoint, seed and weights identifiers not reported.
properties.encoder: AE/VAE terminology is used; default encoder channels [64,128,256], training crop 64^3.
properties.transition: Learned 3D U-Net velocity field trained by flow-matching velocity regression between longitudinal latent endpoints.
properties.conditioning: Start time, current sample time, end query time and patient attributes; sex, age and clinical status are described. Condition MLPs generate AdaLN parameters in decoder layers.
properties.inference: Encode one observed baseline scan, repeatedly advance the latent state by explicit Euler updates, then decode the requested future MRI.
properties.default_pretrained_encoder: The authors explicitly state that the default AE is not pretrained.
properties.auxiliary_configuration_boundary: The separately reported MAISI-initialization result is not assigned to the default model.
properties.prediction_uncertainty_boundary: The displayed inference path is deterministic conditional on its initialized latent state. VAE terminology and stochastic-flow preliminaries do not establish a sampled predictive distribution, calibrated uncertainty or a validated decomposition.
properties.action_interface: The documented forecast interface contains no treatment or other settable clinical action.
properties.planning_interface: No optimizer or policy selects clinical actions in the documented system.

properties.composition: Serial encoder → propagated latent state → learned velocity integration → MRI decoder, with time/metadata conditioning.
training_stages: AE training with image reconstruction and ArcRank regularization
implemented_responsibilities: Learned longitudinal transition and image emission
not_established_as_complete_modules: An operational clinical interface or lifecycle service

properties.purpose: Research generation and evaluation of future brain MRI observations over requested longitudinal intervals.
properties.population: Selected longitudinal ADNI, OASIS-3 and AIBL MRI observations; detailed eligibility and counts not reported.
properties.decision_boundary: No evaluated treatment recommendation, actuation or live workflow decision.
properties.clinical_claim_boundary: Clinical interpretability and potential usefulness are author interpretations or motivations, not demonstrated patient benefit.

properties.initialization: z_i = E(x_i) from an observed baseline MRI
properties.persistence: The latent state is carried and updated through repeated numerical integration steps.
properties.training_regularization: Same-patient angular consistency, chronological singular-value ranking, adjacent-time pull penalty and stop-gradient on the earlier representation.
properties.interpretation_claim: Direction preserves patient identity and magnitude represents progression stage.
properties.interpretation_limit: These are imposed representational assumptions, not identified biological coordinates or proof of patient-specific predictive value.
properties.belief_or_filter: No explicit prior/posterior observation-correction filter is established.
properties.history_at_inference: One baseline MRI plus conditioning metadata; no additional history-memory mechanism is specified.

properties.clinical_anchor: Baseline age plus requested future time span; results report future horizons in years.
properties.training_target: Latent endpoint displacement divided by observed time difference, as in equation (12).
properties.integration: Example dt = 0.01; the physical units or normalization of this numerical step are not specified.
properties.semantic_ambiguity: The paper alternately describes [0,T] as an explicit future time gap and a progression coordinate rather than physical clock time.
properties.separate_optimization_coordinates: AE training: 300 epochs. Flow training: 200 epochs. Neither is a clinical horizon.

properties.coordinate: Longitudinal MRI progression anchored to acquisition-time differences and queried elapsed years.
properties.implemented_transition: z_next = z_current + dt * v_theta(z_current,current_time), with additional described conditioning.
properties.emission: AE decoder maps terminal latent to MRI.
properties.action_conditioning: No action input in the fully described default forecast mechanism.
properties.mechanistic_scope: Geometric and chronological representation regularization, not a physiological conservation law or identified causal disease mechanism.

properties.responsibility: Encode observed MRI into a continuous latent and reconstruct MRI during first-stage training.
properties.completeness_boundary: Supports M2 encoding; no complete modality-availability or foundation-model robustness service is established.

properties.responsibility: Initialize and carry the latent state during a forecast.
properties.completeness_boundary: M3 state-maintenance subrole only; not an established posterior-belief or online-assimilation service.

properties.responsibility: Predict latent velocity and emit a decoded future MRI.
properties.completeness_boundary: M5 transition/emission subroles; interchangeable backends and semantic API compatibility are not established.

properties.responsibility: Integrate the learned latent field to a requested future time and return a forecast MRI.
properties.feedback_mode: Open-loop numerical integration without new measured observations.
properties.completeness_boundary: Supports M6 predictive queries; no tolerance-validated horizon, calibrated trajectory distribution or runtime horizon enforcement is established.

properties.name: ADNI
properties.version_boundary: Paper-described dataset use; no specific ADNI release is invented.

properties.name: AIBL
properties.version_boundary: The 1112 individuals in the cited cohort-paper title are not the present study's sample size.

properties.description: The selected ADNI, AIBL and OASIS-3 observations used in Tables 1–2.
properties.pooling: Whether models were pooled across cohorts or trained separately is not reported.
properties.diagnostic_scope: CN, MCI and AD are depicted in Figure 3; their evaluation counts and distributions are not reported.

properties.description: Unspecified dataset-specific or combined subject subsets underlying Table 6.
properties.horizon_composition: Different horizons use different subject subsets, with fewer subjects at 10–13 years.
properties.comparability_boundary: Not a fixed-cohort longitudinal error curve.

properties.task: Generate a later MRI from a baseline MRI and temporal/metadata conditioning.
preprocessing: Registration to a refined standard brain template
properties.forecast_feedback: Numerical latent-state feedback, not measured re-assimilation.
properties.conditioning_availability: The timing and availability of clinical-status conditioning at inference are not adequately specified.

properties.result_status: Author-reported execution and results; not independently reproduced.

properties.limitation: Horizon-specific counts and matched-cohort comparisons are not reported; year 12 is not tabulated.

properties.dataset: ADNI explicitly named for sex flipping; dataset scope for the status-noise result is not separately specified.
tests: Training-time Gaussian perturbation of clinical-status labels
properties.age_test: Explicitly not performed as a noise-robust attribute test.
properties.interpretation: Metadata sensitivity/robustness checks, not clinical action interventions, fairness validation or uncertainty calibration.

properties.purpose: Auxiliary ∆-RMAE sensitivity to additive Gaussian residual noise.
properties.boundary: Not validation on held-out human data and not direct spatial misregistration simulation.

properties.target: Future brain MRI image and agreement with observed follow-up MRI.
properties.readouts: Image similarity, regional anatomical error and residual progression agreement.
not_equivalent_to: Clinical severity prediction validated as a clinical endpoint

criteria_met: The MRI source cohorts are identified as ADNI, OASIS-3 and AIBL.
The executed preprocessing chain and use of longitudinal acquisition-time differences are described.
criteria_missing: Measurement-level retention of source and transformation lineage is not documented.
Dataset release identities, information-availability timestamps and a complete unit/schema provenance contract are not reported.
assertions.rationale: This is limited source and transformation provenance, not evidence of a complete operational M1 provenance service. Naming cohorts and describing processing do not establish traceability of every derived measurement.

scope.time_horizon: Longitudinal acquisition-time coordinates and elapsed years; raw scanner timestamp precision is not reported.

criteria_met: The longitudinal latent observations are indexed by imaging capture time.
Observed endpoint time differences enter the velocity target, and baseline age plus elapsed span anchors prediction.
assertions.rationale: Presence is scoped to acquisition time at the modeled longitudinal resolution, not device-level timestamp preservation. The numerical integration step dt=0.01 is not treated as a native measurement cadence or as having established physical units.

The supplied full text does not distinguish MRI or metadata acquisition time from the time those inputs became usable. In particular, baseline versus future clinical-status conditioning and its availability are insufficiently specified. This does not establish that future information actually leaked.

No model input encoding measured, missing or invalid MRI/metadata values is described. Skull stripping, image cropping and reported registration failures do not establish missingness or validity masks supplied to the model. Failure exclusions and invalid-input handling remain unspecified.

Elapsed forecast time and baseline age are represented, but per-variable freshness of MRI-derived or clinical metadata measurements is not described. A global prediction interval does not establish time-since-observation tracking for individual inputs.

scope.time_horizon: Requested longitudinal intervals; quantitative forecasting results extend to 13 years.

criteria_met: The training velocity target divides latent displacement by the observed endpoint time difference.
The forecast integrates over the requested interval and conditions on start, current and end query times.
assertions.rationale: Actual elapsed intervals affect prediction rather than being replaced solely by uniform visit indices. This implementation assessment does not establish a dedicated irregular-sampling robustness test, calibrated clinical-time dynamics or accurate prediction at every arbitrary interval. The paper's progression-coordinate qualification remains unresolved.

The method uses observed capture times and externally specified forecast times, but no rule or model for when, whether or why follow-up imaging occurs is reported. Different follow-up availability across subjects is acknowledged without an observation-generation model. Time conditioning alone does not satisfy this feature.

No target-specific temporal-grid witness-preservation audit is reported. Spatial MRI resampling, future-horizon analysis and additive residual-noise sensitivity do not test preservation across sampled values, update patterns, native timing and external acquisition channels.

criteria_met: MRI observations undergo a common spatial and intensity preprocessing chain, including resampling, tissue-contrast normalization and registration to a standard brain template.
criteria_missing: Source-specific measurement mappings, traceable conversion records and the target template/schema identity are not sufficiently specified.
The reported '1.5 mm3 voxels' wording does not unambiguously establish voxel spacing versus volume.
Scanner/protocol harmonization and scanner-invariant representations remain proposed future work rather than evaluated source-invariance mechanisms.
assertions.rationale: Only the imaging-standardization subset is established. It is not a complete semantic/unit harmonization contract, and reported orientation inconsistencies and registration failures limit any assurance of correct mapping.

The random 80/5/15 split is not accompanied by the patient/scan/pair partition unit, longitudinal-overlap controls, training-only preprocessing/template fitting or an information-availability audit. Clinical-status availability is also unclear. A nominal split alone is insufficient, but these omissions do not demonstrate leakage.

No site-local training or query protocol, exchanged artifacts or federated aggregation mechanism is described. Using three clinical datasets does not establish federation. The paper also does not supply the explicit identifiable-record pooling evidence required for the feature's absence rule.

criteria_met: An AE/VAE encoder maps an observed baseline MRI to the latent state consumed by the velocity model.
Executed training settings and encoder-capacity/crop ablations document use of the mapping.
assertions.rationale: The operational observation-to-state mapping is established by the reported pipeline and experiments. The AE/VAE terminology does not establish a posterior-belief filter, complete VAE objective or predictive uncertainty.

Appendix C explicitly states that the default comparison does not use a pretrained AE. This scoped absence concerns transferred encoder parameters in the default configuration, not the separately reported MAISI-initialization experiment.

criteria_met: The flow-training loss regresses a latent-space velocity target constructed from earlier and later encoded MRI representations.
The target is longitudinal latent displacement divided by elapsed time rather than raw MRI reconstruction for this objective.
assertions.rationale: This establishes the functional latent-prediction objective in the dynamics-training stage. It does not classify the AE pretraining as JEPA, imply joint encoder/predictor co-training or exclude a separate observation-reconstruction objective.

criteria_met: The ArcRank representation-learning design includes a positive-margin chronological ranking constraint that penalizes equal or insufficiently separated magnitudes.
A stop-gradient operation is applied in the paired representation objective.
The paper explicitly relates removal of the ranking margin to latent mode collapse.
assertions.rationale: Specified anti-triviality and training-stabilization mechanisms are present in the representation stage used by the predictive system. This is not a proof of collapse prevention: the authors also report collapse for excessive angular-loss weights and convergence problems for excessive ranking weights. No universal or independently validated collapse-free guarantee is assigned.

criteria_met: The first-stage encoder-decoder reconstructs observed MRI, with an image-loss pathway shown in Figure 1.
The reported reconstruction trade-offs and AE configuration experiments document training and use of this reconstruction mapping.
assertions.rationale: Observation reconstruction is an implemented first-stage objective alongside ArcRank. The complete loss formula, weighting and any KL component are insufficiently specified, so no particular reconstruction norm or fully specified VAE objective is inferred. Reconstruction and the separate latent velocity-regression objective coexist.

criteria_met: MRI-derived latent representations interact with separately identified structured patient metadata.
Condition-processing MLPs generate AdaLN parameters applied within the U-Net decoder layers.
Reported metadata perturbation experiments corroborate operational use of the conditioning inputs.
assertions.rationale: The fusion is between imaging representations and structured patient attributes, not between the three MRI datasets. Temporal query embeddings are not counted as another clinical modality. This assertion establishes the implemented interaction, not missing-modality robustness or clinically valid conditioning.

The paper specifies metadata/time conditioning through AdaLN but does not specify availability masks, quality/recency-dependent fusion, or behavior when MRI or conditioning metadata are missing. Sex flipping and clinical-status noise are not missing-modality tests. A requirement that all inputs be present is also not explicitly established, so absence is not asserted.

criteria_met: An observed MRI initializes a defined latent state.
Each numerical transition carries the preceding latent state into the next velocity-field update.
The propagated terminal state is decoded and evaluated against later observed MRI.
assertions.rationale: Persistence is established by the executed latent integration and reported future-observation results, not merely by the presence of an encoder. Numerical integration steps are distinguished from years of follow-up. The evidence does not establish a tolerance-validated horizon or independent patient-level splitting.

No observation-history-conditioned filtering distribution with stated uncertainty semantics is reported. The AE/VAE terminology and stochastic-flow preliminaries do not establish such a belief. Conversely, deterministic propagation conditional on an initialized latent does not resolve the encoder's latent-distribution convention sufficiently to assert that every state representation is exclusively deterministic.

The specified forecast procedure encodes the baseline once, repeatedly propagates its latent state, and decodes the requested endpoint. It contains no operation accepting a newly measured observation to correct a prior prediction. This is scoped absence of a correction operation in the documented open-loop query, not a claim that the architecture could never be extended with filtering.

Within the fully described inference episode, subsequent states derive from the baseline initialization and generated latent updates, without later measured scans entering the rollout. Numerical state updates are not assimilation of arriving evidence. Reinitializing a separate forecast from another scan would not itself demonstrate sequential assimilation.

The reported inference algorithm evaluates the trained encoder, condition-processing networks, velocity field and decoder; it updates the latent state rather than fitting individual parameters or model weights. Patient-specificity is supplied through baseline representations, metadata and training regularization. No parameter-fitting operation occurs in this documented inference path. This assertion does not exclude an unreported alternative adaptation procedure.

The demonstrated output is future MRI generation. Multiple horizons, several image-error metrics and t-SNE coloring by diagnosis do not establish a second typed task/readout sharing the same learned state checkpoint. The paper also does not document separately trained task-specific state models that would establish the feature's negative criterion.

criteria_met: Conditioning is removed in an unconditional-versus-conditional comparison against the MRI prediction targets.
Angular, ranking and combined latent-representation training strategies are compared using image and progression-error metrics.
AE capacity and crop-size variants are evaluated against forecasting metrics.
assertions.rationale: These are relevant representation/input ablations under this feature's operational definition, not proof that the learned state contains every transition determinant. Outcomes are metric-dependent: ArcRank with temporal sampling improves several reported means but has lower SSIM than ArcRank with normalized sampling. No history-length sufficiency, causal sufficiency or clinical decision-sufficiency conclusion follows.

scope.time_horizon: Inference initialized from one observed MRI

assertions.rationale: The documented inference interface uses one supplied baseline MRI and attributes/time queries, rather than conditioning on a sequence of earlier individual scans or actions. Longitudinal pairs supervise training but are not a patient's inference-time history. Here baseline conditioning is distinguished from conditioning on history preceding that supplied snapshot, consistent with the feature's explicit current-snapshot exclusion.

No matched individual-history swap/withholding or population-prior forecast control is reported. Patient clustering, ArcRank ablations, general conditioning removal and sex/status perturbations do not isolate the added predictive value of the correct individual's information without leakage. Personalization is claimed and structurally encouraged, but the specified audit is not established.

criteria_met: ArcRank explicitly aligns the directions of longitudinal representations belonging to the same patient.
The authors assign latent direction the role of preserving patient identity.
The regularizer is part of the reported trained configuration, not solely a proposed extension.
assertions.rationale: This establishes an implemented identity-consistency loss mechanism. It does not establish anatomically faithful identity preservation at every generated horizon. The reported ablations and t-SNE visualization do not substitute for a dedicated decoded-identity violation test.

criteria_met: The authors document a global semantic interpretation of latent direction as patient identity and magnitude as progression stage.
SVD-derived components and t-SNE plots provide an inspectable representation-level visualization.
Figure 3 displays ADNI representations colored by patient identity and diagnosis.
criteria_missing: The proposed progression-stage interpretation is not resolved into a validated mapping to measured clinical severity; chronology is imposed and clinical-status conditioning creates a stage-specific interpretation ambiguity.
No readable mapping from propagated latent components to identified anatomical or physiological variables is supplied.
assertions.rationale: The representation has inspectable global structure, but qualitative projected clustering does not make the full state physiologically interpretable. No clinician interpretation study or clinical severity readout is inferred.

The specified transition uses the current propagated latent, time and patient attributes. It contains no recurrent history store, earlier-observation context window or external memory beyond that supplied state. Sinusoidal time embeddings and numerical state persistence are not additional observation-history memory. This is not a finding that a Markov state is intrinsically inadequate.

The documented prediction interface comprises an MRI-derived latent, temporal queries and patient attributes, with no settable treatment, acquisition command or other intervention separated from observed state. Flipping sex and perturbing diagnostic status are metadata sensitivity experiments, not executable clinical actions. A requested forecast time specifies the observation target rather than an intervention on the modeled patient.

assertions.applicability_reason: The documented model is an actionless observational MRI forecaster. Because its assessed prediction interface has no clinical action variable, distinguishing action roles and effect channels within an action vocabulary is inapplicable to this configuration.
assertions.rationale: This dependency-specific inapplicability does not treat metadata as an uninterpreted action vector and does not extend to any future treatment-conditioned version.

Delta-LFM defines a continuous-time latent velocity field over [0, T] (Eqs. 12-15, p. 5) integrated via Euler updates z_{i+dt} = z_i + dt * v_theta(z_i, t_i), ablated against [0,1] sampling (Table 3, p. 8), and quantitatively evaluated across 1-11 and 13-year horizons (Table 6, p. 15).

The latent velocity field v_theta is implemented as a learned 3D U-Net with AdaLN conditioning trained with AdamW via latent flow matching (p. 5, Appendix A-B p. 14) and evaluated across ADNI, AIBL, and OASIS-3 (Tables 1-2, pp. 7-8).

relation_assertions.rationale: Version identification uses the supplied title-page text and registry hash; the hash was not independently recomputed.
Reported executed training and forecasting establish implementation reporting, not independently inspected code.

scope.population: Longitudinal brain MRI observations from ADNI, AIBL and OASIS-3

relation_assertions.rationale: The evolving entity is brain anatomy represented by MRI latents; neither multimodal metadata nor multiple datasets establishes multiscale coupling.
This is a reviewer-defined boundary around the evaluated research use, not an author-specified clinical deployment.
Encoding subrole, not complete M2 assurance or missing-modality capability.
Carried latent-state subrole only; no posterior-belief or propagate-correct claim.
Learned transition/emission responsibility only; pluggable-backend compatibility is not established.
Open-loop predictive-query subrole; not a calibrated distribution service or horizon guarantee.
Cohort source and split are reported; eligibility counts, split independence and pooling remain unresolved.

scope.time_horizon: Reported quantitative forecasts at 1–11 and 13 years

relation_assertions.rationale: Results evaluate later MRI observations following learned latent-state evolution. Metadata edits are not settable clinical actions, so they do not establish L2/L3. No model-coupled decision optimizer establishes L4.

A stated train/validation/test split and reported tests on actual human MRI cohorts support retrospective internal evaluation. This does not establish patient-disjointness, leakage control, successful clinical validation or external independence. Table 7's synthetic noise test is not used to establish R2.

Verified core-method membership supports a temporal-prediction research profile. M6 and G03 are additionally relevant because the evaluated queries span multiple years. BP_MULTI is not assigned because probabilistic forecast semantics and guarantees are not established.

evidence_fragments.content: [paraphrase (visual p.3)] Figure 1 overview (p. 3): Stage A (Latent Space) encodes longitudinal MRIs via E(.) into latent z, reconstructs via D(.), and applies SVD (z = U Sigma V^T) with ArcRank Loss (push/pull along patient vector z_c); Stage B (Delta-Latent Flow Matching) depicts Forward Stochastic Flow and Learned Deterministic Flow (d z_hat_t = E[v_theta(z_t | z_i, z_j)] dt) over horizon T/dt.

Inference.Given an input statex i observed at timeti, the encoder maps it to a latent representation
zi. To predict the target statex j at a later timet j,∆-LFM integrates the learned velocity field
forward in time. Specifically, we fix a discretization step size dt >0(e.g., dt= 0.01), so that the
total number of integration steps is
N= tj −t i
dt .(14)
At each step, the latent state is updated according to the learned dynamics
zi+dt =z i +dt·v θ(zi, ti),(15)
with time advanced ast i+dt =t i +dt. Repeated application of this update yields an approximation
of the latent state att j, which is then decoded to produce the predicted observation ˆxj.

locator.section_or_table: §3.4, latent-space reasoning and temporal uneven progression

evidence_fragments.content:
Temporal uneven progression.We formulate flow matching (FM) over the interval[0, T], inter-
preting the index as a progression coordinate rather than physical clock time. However, although
this formulation accounts for time differences, it implicitly assumes that progression is evenly dis-
tributed along the disease trajectory. In practice, progression is often uneven: extended periods of
stability may be punctuated by sudden changes, or vice versa. The constant-velocity assumption in
FM fails to capture this heterogeneity, effectively treating patient scans as uniformly spaced along
the trajectory. To address this limitation, we introduce conditioning on the target timeTtogether
with patient-specific attributes (e.g., sex, age, and clinical status) to enable the model to capture
heterogeneous progression patterns that vary substantially over time.

We build our study on three major Alzheimer’s disease (AD) cohorts: ADNI (Petersen et al., 2010),
OASIS-3 (LaMontagne et al., 2019), and AIBL (Ellis et al., 2009). Every MRI undergoes the same
preprocessing pipeline: N4 bias correction (Tustison et al., 2010), skull stripping (Hoopes et al.,
2022), resampling to 1.5 mm3 voxels. We then normalize tissue contrasts and register all scans to a
refined standard brain template. We use a random 80/5/15 split for train/validation/test.

0.0025–0.0075are stable across runs, withλ arc = 0.0075noticeably degrading AE reconstruction.
We therefore setλ arc = 0.005as a compromise, trading a small decrease in AE reconstruction for

Forλ rank, values above0.05hinder convergence, whereas the range0.005–0.02yields similar be-
havior. We chooseλ rank = 0.01, which gives a slight PSNR gain (+0.05).
Speed AnalysisArcRank involves an SVD operation, which is computational expensive. In prac-
tice, we usetorch.linalg.svd(z, full matrices=False), which gives a6×speedup
compared to the full matrices variant (0.0552s→0.0092s on average over 50 runs). Overall, Ar-
cRank increases AE training time by∼40%(1.4×), which we regard as a reasonable overhead
given the resulting performance gains.

We adopt the AdamW optimizer (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017) for all experiments. For the autoen-
coder (AE) and 3D U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015), we trained with a learning rate of1×10 −3
and a batch size of2for 300 epochs. For the flow matching model based on the 3D U-Net, we used
a reduced learning rate of3×10 −5 with a larger batch size of4for 200 epochs.

Building on this, and inspired by BrLP (Puglisi et al., 2024), we introduceexplicit control signals
that combine patient-specific attributes with temporal queries. In particular, we condition the model
not only on the start time, the current sample time, and the end query time, but also on the pa-
tient attributes. This design enables the model to incorporate both subject-specific and task-specific
information when shaping the generative trajectory.
To inject these conditional signals into the U-Net backbone, we explored three strategies: (1) Ad-
ditive biasing, (2) Cross-attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) and (3) Adaptive Layer Normalization
(AdaLN) (Raffel et al., 2020).
Among these approaches, our experiments show that AdaLN is most effective with our temporal
sampling over the interval[0, T]. It adapts the network representation in a temporally aware and
context-sensitive manner, allowing the generative process to be steered smoothly by patient attributes
and target query times.
The implementation of AdaLN is realized through an initial one-layer MLP that processes the condi-
tion signals, followed by additional MLPs at each U-Net decoder layer to generate the corresponding
AdaLN modulation parameters.

We do not use deeper or wider AEs, as these configurations lead to out-of-memory (OOM) errors on
our RTX A6000 GPU (48 GB). Based on the above results, we use channels[64,128,256]and crop
size64 3 as our default configuration. Larger crops (e.g.,72 3) also result in OOM on our hardware.
To keep the comparison with baselines fair, we do not use a pretrained AE, although initializing with
MAISI (Guo et al., 2025) can further improve PSNR (from 30.04 to 31.97 for[64,128,256]).

Beyond 6 years, however, all metrics exhibit gradual degradation. PSNR and SSIM decline steadily,
dropping to 28 dB and below 91% by year 10, and further to 26.98 dB / 89.96% at year 13. Con-
currently, Region MAE and∆-RMAE increase monotonically, indicating that both absolute errors
in regional values and their temporal progression deviate more strongly with longer horizons. No-
tably, the sharp rise in∆-RMAE after year 10 (>0.50) highlights a growing difficulty in capturing
long-term progression trends.
We also observe that the prediction trend is not strictly linear as the prediction horizon increases.
This is mainly because different time horizons are estimated from different subsets of subjects.
In particular, fewer subjects have follow-up data at 10–13 years compared to 1–5 years, which
introduces higher variability and heterogeneity, leading to slightly inconsistent trends.

evidence_fragments.content:
Sex.To evaluate robustness with respect to sex, we intentionally flipped the sex attribute and
re-evaluated the model. On ADNI, performance changed only marginally, from PSNR/SSIM of
30.59/94.62to30.12/94.47, indicating limited sensitivity to this source of label noise.
Clinical status.In clinical practice, diagnostic labels are inherently noisy. To reflect this, we inject
Gaussian noise into the clinical status during training to model diagnostic uncertainty. Specifically,
we use zero-mean Gaussian noise with standard deviation equal to one-third of the status class
interval (interval= 3).
Under perturbed status labels, performance remains reasonable, with PSNR/SSIM degrading only
slightly from30.59/94.62to29.81/93.58, demonstrating robustness to clinically realistic label
noise.

Age.Age serves as the temporal anchor for longitudinal prediction, as future timepoints are de-
fined by (baseline age+time span). Injecting noise into age would therefore shift the implied
prediction timepoint, so that the generated image no longer corresponds to a meaningful clinical
follow-up. Such an ablation would be difficult to interpret, and for this reason we do not treat age as
a noise-robust attribute.

Dataset processing limitation.Although we followed standard MRI preprocessing protocols, vari-
ations across scanners and acquisition protocols introduce substantial heterogeneity in the data. Such
differences may affect the stability of model training and the reliability of generated outputs. Fur-
thermore, we identified occasional metadata inconsistencies (e.g., mislabeling of imaging orienta-
tion), which led to registration failures in certain cases. While these issues were infrequent, they
highlight the importance of rigorous data curation and quality control in longitudinal imaging re-
search. Future work may benefit from harmonization techniques or scanner-invariant representations
to further mitigate such variability.

First, the incorporation of explicit anatomical information could enable more fine-grained modeling
of disease progression. By constraining generation with structure-aware priors (e.g., hippocampus,
ventricles, cortical regions), the model may better capture local pathological changes while preserv-
ing biological plausibility.
Second, beyond modeling each patient in isolation, future work may explore leveraging inter-patient
disease trend similarity and dissimilarity. Identifying cohorts of patients with comparable progres-
sion patterns may enable transfer of knowledge across individuals, while simultaneously capturing
unique patient-specific deviations. In addition, modeling nonlinear progression dynamics remains
an important direction for future work.
Addressing dataset heterogeneity remains another critical challenge. Future works may investigate
harmonization techniques and scanner-invariant representations to mitigate variability introduced
by different acquisition protocols and hardware. Such advances will be essential for scaling the
framework to large, multi-center cohorts and for ensuring robust generalization in real-world clinical
applications.

limitations: This is automated API model review, including a skeptical second-pass synthesis of the supplied page reviews against the full supplied text. It is not independent human verification, independent replication or a separately certified external assessment.

All 17 physical pages of supplied text were read. Raw page-image files were not available in this call; visual findings rely on the supplied page-by-page image-review notes and are not a new direct image inspection.

The source path, availability, page count and PDF hash come from the supplied source record. No filesystem access, hash recomputation, repository inspection or external bibliographic verification was performed.
Feature assertions are intentionally empty as requested. This is not a completed 128-feature annotation or a completed feature-coverage validation.
No executable JSON Schema validator, semantic checker or KG assembler was run. The annotation has not been admitted to a canonical graph or saved to project files.
The source record year 2025 differs from the read arXiv v4 date and ICLR 2026 header. These values are preserved rather than silently conflated.
Selected patient, scan, longitudinal-pair and institution counts, eligibility criteria and dataset release versions are not reported. Citation-title cohort counts cannot supply them.
The random 80/5/15 split does not specify its patient/scan/pair unit. Patient independence, longitudinal overlap, preprocessing leakage and independent external validation remain unresolved.
It is not clear whether cohorts were pooled or models were fitted separately. Three benchmark names alone do not establish external validation.

Clinical-status conditioning is described, but the availability time and whether baseline or future status is used are not adequately specified. Statements that severity/diagnosis was unused in training may refer to the AE rather than flow stage; this distinction requires clarification.

The paper mixes elapsed-time and progression-coordinate descriptions. The units/normalization of dt=0.01, noninteger integration counts, final partial steps and numerical error controls are not specified.

Equation (13)'s network notation and intermediate-state sampling are not fully reconciled with the explicit state/time inference field. Claims of avoiding long integrations or solver sensitivity are not established by the reported Euler description or a solver ablation.

Chronological monotonicity and a straight latent trajectory are modeling assumptions, not universal properties of clinical disease. The authors acknowledge uneven progression and identify nonlinear progression as future work.
Latent tensor shape, SVD axes/reshaping, basis sign/degeneracy handling, ranking margin value, pair sampling and full loss normalization are insufficiently specified.

The complete AE/VAE reconstruction/KL objective and latent sampling convention are not sufficiently detailed to establish predictive uncertainty. Stochastic-flow background is not an evaluated stochastic clinical forecast.
t-SNE clustering and same-patient regularization do not establish patient-history benefit under matched swapped/withheld-history or population-prior forecasting controls.

Figure 2 is a selected qualitative example with percentile-scaled residuals and no numeric colorbar; shared scaling is unclear. Its caption's odd/even column wording is ambiguous when the ground-truth column is counted.
Figure 4 displays generated trajectories and baseline-relative residuals, not observed future scans or forecast-error maps. It does not establish accurate nine-year prediction by itself.
Region MAE units, normalization, segmentation procedure and aggregation are not sufficiently reported. Table 1–2 SDs lack a clear sampling unit; Table 6 does not explicitly identify its ± statistic.

The reported best-comparator and monotonic-degradation statements conflict with tabulated metric-specific results. All source numbers are retained without replacing them with reviewer-computed percentages.

Table 6 uses different subject subsets across horizons and fewer long-follow-up subjects. Counts are not reported, year 12 is omitted, and the curve cannot isolate within-cohort compounding model error.
Thirteen years is a maximum reported quantitative horizon, not an effective or clinically acceptable horizon. No acceptance tolerance, risk criterion or horizon enforcement is established.
∆-RMAE measures imaging-residual agreement, not disease-specific causal change. Registration, normal aging, intensity and acquisition differences can contribute to residuals.
∆-RMAE zero-denominator stabilization and complete voxel/region/subject reduction are not specified. The claimed noise-induced effective upper-bound reduction is not a general mathematical guarantee.

Table 7 starts at a saturated noiseless ∆-RMAE of 2.0. Its sample size, noise units, residual distribution and repetitions are not reported; additive residual noise does not validate spatial-registration robustness or preserved model rankings.
Metadata perturbations do not establish fairness, causal sex effects, treatment intervention fidelity or clinical diagnostic-error realism. Age noise was explicitly not tested.

Ablations do not independently isolate every component, including the pull term, stop-gradient, each metadata variable and nonlinear versus straight-line trajectories. AdaLN superiority lacks a reported numerical three-strategy comparison.
Hyperparameter collapse and convergence statements lack run counts, dispersions and explicit collapse definitions. Larger AE/crop configurations caused OOM on the reported 48 GB RTX A6000.
SVD microbenchmark speedup and total AE training overhead have different denominators. End-to-end forecast inference latency, total training hours and full model parameter count are not reported.

The authors acknowledge AD-only scope, scanner/protocol heterogeneity and occasional orientation-metadata-related registration failures. Failure denominators, exclusions and effects on reported results are not given.

Anatomical structure constraints, inter-patient trend transfer, brain-tumor extension, nonlinear disease dynamics and scanner-invariant harmonization are future work, not inherited implementation capabilities.
